questions.stem: A 52-year-old client who drinks about a fifth of vodka daily had the last drink at 2200 last night and is admitted for an elective knee replacement at 0700. The client asks when the "shakes" might start. When should the nurse expect early withdrawal symptoms to begin?

options.text: Between about 6 and 24 hours after the last drink
About 1 week after the last drink, once the alcohol has fully cleared
After 72 hours, at the same time as the risk of delirium tremens
Within 30 minutes of the last drink

rationale.correct: Alcohol withdrawal: early signs at 6 to 24 hours, seizures at 12 to 48 hours, delirium tremens at 48 to 96 hours.

perOption.a: Early withdrawal (tremor, anxiety, tachycardia) begins within a day.
perOption.b: Withdrawal begins much sooner.
perOption.c: Delirium tremens comes later than early withdrawal signs.
perOption.d: There is a delay of hours.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Predict the timing of alcohol withdrawal.

questions.stem: Three days after admission for a hip fracture, a client with heavy daily alcohol use is confused, sweating and picking at bugs on the sheets. The temperature is 38.4 °C (101.1 °F), the heart rate is 128/min and the blood pressure is 176/102 mm Hg. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV benzodiazepines, seizure precautions and close monitoring
Haloperidol as the only medicine to control the hallucinations
Blood cultures and antibiotics for a new infection
Fluid restriction to prevent overload with the high blood pressure

rationale.correct: Delirium tremens: benzodiazepines, fluids, electrolytes, thiamine and a safe environment.

perOption.a: These signs show delirium tremens, a medical emergency treated with benzodiazepines.
perOption.b: Antipsychotics alone can lower the seizure threshold and do not treat withdrawal.
perOption.c: Infection should be considered, but the picture and timing fit delirium tremens.
perOption.d: Clients in withdrawal are often dehydrated.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client admitted for pancreatitis has a history of heavy alcohol use. The provider orders lorazepam per the CIWA-Ar protocol. A new nurse asks what the CIWA-Ar score is used for. What should the charge nurse explain?

options.text: It rates withdrawal severity so medicine is given when symptoms call for it
It confirms the diagnosis of alcohol use disorder for the chart
It estimates the blood alcohol level from the client's symptoms
It screens the client for suicide risk during withdrawal

rationale.correct: Use CIWA-Ar for symptom-triggered treatment of alcohol withdrawal.

perOption.a: Scores guide symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing.
perOption.b: It measures withdrawal, not the disorder.
perOption.c: Blood alcohol is a lab test.
perOption.d: Other tools assess suicide risk.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A thin, malnourished client with alcohol use disorder is brought in confused, with an unsteady, wide-based gait and jerking eye movements. The fingerstick glucose is 58 mg/dL. The provider orders thiamine, folic acid, a multivitamin and IV dextrose 50%. Which should the nurse give first?

options.text: Thiamine 100 mg IV
Dextrose 50% IV push
Folic acid 1 mg IV
A multivitamin in the IV fluid

rationale.correct: Give thiamine before glucose in at-risk clients to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, nystagmus).

perOption.a: Giving glucose before thiamine can bring on or worsen Wernicke encephalopathy, and these signs suggest it is already present.
perOption.b: Unless the hypoglycemia is severe and the client is unresponsive, thiamine is given just before or with the glucose.
perOption.c: This helps but is not the priority before glucose.
perOption.d: This is added later.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with alcohol use disorder who has been sober for 2 weeks is starting disulfiram 250 mg daily. The client cooks often and uses a mouthwash after meals. Which statement shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll check labels and skip mouthwash or sauces with alcohol."
"One beer with dinner should be fine at this dose."
"If I want a drink, I'll skip that day's dose first."
"This pill will take away my cravings for alcohol."

rationale.correct: Disulfiram: avoid all hidden alcohol sources; the reaction includes flushing, vomiting and hypotension.

perOption.a: Even small amounts of hidden alcohol cause a severe reaction.
perOption.b: Any alcohol causes a reaction.
perOption.c: The effect lasts up to 2 weeks after the last dose.
perOption.d: It deters drinking; it does not reduce cravings.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client who uses heroin daily was arrested 18 hours ago and is brought from jail to the emergency department. Which group of findings is most consistent with opioid withdrawal?

options.text: Yawning, runny nose, dilated pupils and diarrhea
Pinpoint pupils, slow breathing and drowsiness
Seizures, visual hallucinations and high fever
Bradycardia, low blood pressure and dry skin

rationale.correct: Opioid withdrawal: flu-like symptoms, mydriasis, piloerection, GI upset and cravings.

perOption.a: These are typical; they are very uncomfortable but rarely life-threatening.
perOption.b: These suggest opioid intoxication or overdose.
perOption.c: These are more typical of alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal.
perOption.d: Withdrawal causes tachycardia, hypertension and sweating.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with opioid use disorder who last injected heroin 4 hours ago wants to start buprenorphine-naloxone today in the clinic. The client's pupils are small and the client is drowsy but easy to wake. The Clinical Opiate Withdrawal Scale (COWS) score is 2. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Wait to give the first dose until withdrawal signs appear
Give the first dose now so that the client does not leave the clinic
Give a dose of naloxone first to clear the heroin
Delay the start until the client has been opioid-free for 30 days

rationale.correct: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist; start it when withdrawal is already present (often COWS 8 to 12 or more).

perOption.a: Buprenorphine given while full agonists are still active can trigger sudden (precipitated) withdrawal.
perOption.b: This risks precipitated withdrawal.
perOption.c: This would cause severe withdrawal.
perOption.d: Buprenorphine can be started once mild to moderate withdrawal is present.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client completing a residential program for opioid use disorder plans to start extended-release naltrexone injections before discharge. The client used oxycodone 3 days ago. What must the nurse confirm before the first injection?

options.text: The client has been opioid-free for 7 to 10 days
The client is taking a small dose of oxycodone to prevent cravings
The client has a normal blood glucose level
The client has signed up for a methadone program

rationale.correct: Naltrexone is an opioid antagonist; the client must be opioid-free first, confirmed by history and urine testing.

perOption.a: Naltrexone blocks opioids and causes severe withdrawal if opioids are still in the body.
perOption.b: Opioids must be stopped before naltrexone.
perOption.c: This is not the key requirement.
perOption.d: Methadone is a full agonist and cannot be used with naltrexone.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Prepare a client to start naltrexone.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old is found unresponsive in a restroom with a syringe nearby. The respiratory rate is 6/min, the pupils are pinpoint, the SpO2 is 80% and the fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL. After bag-valve-mask ventilation begins, which medicine should the nurse prepare to give?

options.text: Naloxone intranasal
Flumazenil IV push
Dextrose 50% IV push
Lorazepam IV push

rationale.correct: Opioid overdose: support breathing and give naloxone; watch for re-sedation as it wears off.

perOption.a: Pinpoint pupils, coma and slow breathing are typical of opioid overdose.
perOption.b: This reverses benzodiazepines and can cause seizures; the picture fits opioids.
perOption.c: The glucose is normal.
perOption.d: This would deepen the respiratory depression.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old who used cocaine at a party 1 hour ago comes to the emergency department with crushing chest pain. The heart rate is 132/min, the blood pressure is 188/108 mm Hg, the temperature is 38.2 °C (100.8 °F) and the pupils are dilated. What is the nurse's main concern?

options.text: Myocardial ischemia from coronary vasospasm
Respiratory depression from the drug
A panic attack brought on by the stimulant effect
Withdrawal seizures as the drug wears off

rationale.correct: Stimulant toxicity: tachycardia, hypertension, chest pain, hyperthermia and agitation; benzodiazepines are first-line and beta-blockers are avoided.

perOption.a: Cocaine causes coronary vasospasm, ischemia and dysrhythmias, even in young adults.
perOption.b: This is more typical of opioids.
perOption.c: Chest pain after cocaine is cardiac until proven otherwise.
perOption.d: Cocaine withdrawal causes fatigue and depression, not seizures.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client admitted with alcoholic liver disease and ascites tells the nurse, "I don't have a drinking problem. I only drink beer, and I can stop anytime I want." Which defense mechanism is the client using?

options.text: Denial
Sublimation
Projection
Regression

rationale.correct: Denial is a major barrier to treatment in substance use disorders.

perOption.a: Refusing to acknowledge the problem is common in substance use.
perOption.b: This channels impulses into acceptable activities.
perOption.c: This attributes one's feelings to others.
perOption.d: This is returning to earlier behavior.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client with alcohol use disorder tells the nurse, "When he's hungover, I call his boss and say he has the flu. I also pay off his bar tab so we don't get calls at home." Which behavior is the spouse describing?

options.text: Enabling
Healthy support
Detachment
A planned intervention

rationale.correct: Families benefit from support groups such as Al-Anon to stop enabling.

perOption.a: Protecting the client from consequences allows the drinking to continue.
perOption.b: This protects the drinking, not the client's health.
perOption.c: Detachment means stepping back from the drinker's choices.
perOption.d: An intervention confronts the drinking.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: During an admission interview, the nurse uses the CAGE questionnaire to screen a client for alcohol use. Which question is part of the CAGE screening tool?

options.text: "Have you ever felt you should cut down on your drinking?"
"How many drinks do you usually have on a weekday?"
"Do you drink more on weekends than during the week?"
"How old were you when you had your first alcoholic drink?"

rationale.correct: CAGE: Cut down, Annoyed, Guilty, Eye-opener; two or more yes answers suggest a problem.

perOption.a: C = Cut down.
perOption.b: This is a quantity question, not a CAGE item.
perOption.c: This is not a CAGE item.
perOption.d: This is not a CAGE item.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old with a history of mild memory loss is admitted with a urinary tract infection and new confusion. For each feature, indicate whether it is more typical of delirium or dementia.

rows.text: Sudden onset over hours to days
Level of awareness that changes during the day
Often clears when the cause is treated
Trouble finding words that has slowly worsened

rationale.correct: Delirium: acute, fluctuating, inattentive, often reversible. Dementia: gradual and progressive.

perOption.r2:c1: Fluctuating awareness is typical of delirium.
perOption.r2:c2: Consciousness is usually stable in dementia until late.
perOption.r4:c1: Delirium often resolves when the cause is treated.
perOption.r5:c1: Inattention is a core feature of delirium.
perOption.r5:c2: Attention is often preserved early in dementia.
perOption.r6:c2: Slowly progressive word-finding trouble fits dementia.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 88-year-old resident with advanced Alzheimer's disease walks to the nurses' station every afternoon asking, "Where's my mother? She's coming to take me home." The resident's mother died 30 years ago. What is the best response?

options.text: "You're thinking about your mother. Tell me about her."
"Your mother died many years ago. You live here now."
"She called and said she'll be here after dinner."
"You asked that yesterday. Please go back to your room."

rationale.correct: Use validation and redirection in advanced dementia; avoid arguing.

perOption.a: Validation addresses the feelings without arguing.
perOption.b: Repeated reorientation to a painful fact causes fresh grief each time.
perOption.c: This is dishonest and may increase agitation later.
perOption.d: This is dismissive.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Communicate with a client who has dementia.

questions.stem: A resident with moderate dementia is calm in the morning but becomes confused, restless and tries to leave the unit around 1600 each day. Staff change shifts at 1500, and family visits often happen around 1600. Which intervention is most likely to help?

options.text: Keep a set routine and bright light in the late afternoon
Schedule baths and family visits for the late afternoon
Dim the lights early to encourage an early bedtime
Give a sedative-hypnotic at 1500 each day before symptoms start

rationale.correct: Sundowning: routine, daytime activity, lighting and a calm evening environment.

perOption.a: Structure and good lighting reduce sundowning.
perOption.b: This adds stimulation at the hardest time of day.
perOption.c: Shadows and low light can increase confusion.
perOption.d: Sedatives increase falls and confusion in older adults.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The adult child of a client with Alzheimer's disease reports that the client left the house twice this week at night and was found by neighbors. The client lives with the adult child. Which safety measure should the nurse recommend?

options.text: Door alarms and a medical ID bracelet for the client
Locking the client in the bedroom from the outside at night
Giving diphenhydramine at bedtime to help the client sleep
Taking away the clocks and calendars to reduce distress

rationale.correct: Wandering: secure the environment, use ID, alarms and supervised walking.

perOption.a: These reduce the risk of the client getting lost and help others return the client home.
perOption.b: This is unsafe and a fire hazard.
perOption.c: Anticholinergics increase confusion and falls.
perOption.d: Clocks and calendars help orientation.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Promote safety for a client who wanders.

questions.stem: A 79-year-old client with Alzheimer's disease started donepezil 5 mg at bedtime 3 weeks ago. The adult child reports the client had mild nausea the first week, now has vivid dreams and nearly fainted twice this week. Which finding should the nurse report to the provider right away?

options.text: A heart rate of 48/min with near-fainting
Mild nausea during the first week of treatment
Vivid dreams since starting the medicine at bedtime
Slightly better recall of family members' names

rationale.correct: Donepezil: GI upset, bradycardia, syncope and vivid dreams.

perOption.a: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia and syncope, which risk falls and injury.
perOption.b: This is common and often improves.
perOption.c: This is a common effect; a morning dose may help.
perOption.d: This is the intended effect.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old with ADHD is starting methylphenidate 5 mg twice daily. The parent says the child already eats little and has trouble falling asleep. Which instruction should the nurse give?

options.text: Give doses at breakfast and lunch; track sleep and weight
Give the second dose at bedtime so it lasts through the night
Skip doses on weekends whenever the child seems calmer
Expect the child to gain weight once the medicine starts

rationale.correct: Stimulants: morning dosing, monitor height, weight, heart rate and blood pressure; store securely.

perOption.a: Stimulants can cause insomnia and reduced appetite; dosing with meals early in the day helps.
perOption.b: A late dose causes insomnia.
perOption.c: Drug holidays are planned with the provider.
perOption.d: Appetite and weight often decrease.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with autism spectrum disorder who speaks a few words is admitted for an appendectomy. The parent says the child covers the ears at loud sounds and gets upset when routines change. Which intervention is most helpful?

options.text: Ask the parent about routines and keep the room quiet
Rotate nurses each shift so the child gets used to new people
Place the child in a shared room near the busy playroom
Ask the child to look at the nurse during each procedure

rationale.correct: Autism: routine, consistent caregivers, reduced stimulation and parents' input on preferences.

perOption.a: Predictability and low stimulation reduce distress; parents know the child's needs.
perOption.b: Consistent caregivers are important.
perOption.c: Overstimulation increases distress.
perOption.d: Insisting on eye contact may increase anxiety.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Plan care for a child with autism.

questions.stem: A client who started varenicline 3 weeks ago to quit smoking calls the clinic. The client has had nausea and vivid dreams and now says, "I've been feeling hopeless, and I don't really see the point of anything." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask about suicidal thoughts and tell the client to stop the drug
Reassure the client that low mood is common when quitting nicotine
Suggest taking the dose with food to reduce the nausea
Recommend adding a nicotine patch to ease the cravings

rationale.correct: Varenicline: monitor mood and behavior; stop and report agitation, depression or suicidal thoughts. Nausea and vivid dreams are common.

perOption.a: Varenicline can cause neuropsychiatric effects; safety is assessed and the drug stopped pending provider review.
perOption.b: Hopelessness on varenicline needs urgent evaluation.
perOption.c: This misses the mood change.
perOption.d: This does not address the mood change.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client admitted with pneumonia had the last drink of alcohol 36 hours ago. The nurse reviews the flowsheet. Highlight the findings that indicate worsening alcohol withdrawal.

cells: Coarse tremor when arms are held out
Sees insects crawling on the wall
Crackles in the right lower lobe

rationale.correct: Watch for rising vital signs, tremor, hallucinations and confusion.

perOption.r3: Tremor is a sign of withdrawal.
perOption.r6: This is expected with the pneumonia.

references: Psychiatric-mental health nursing texts (e.g. Varcarolis; Halter)
